doc.title: Oliver Nelson Jr. interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 10, 2020

title: Song titles and the music catalogue
summary: Boxes of scores to catalogue, and titles like One for Brucie, Teenie's Blues and Miss Fine named for family, including his aunt Leontine LaCoste.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: What about song titles? Did he ever have music that he had written, original music, that he had trouble thinking what do I call this?

Well it’s interesting, he would think of those when they had to go on a record. But I’ve got a ton of scores of N-201s and 302s and that kind of, and I have to sit down and figure out a lot of times what they were. And some of this stuff has never been done. And I’ve got boxes and boxes of music and I’ve had one of my students kind of help me catalogue stuff but then Covid came around so she can’t even come to the house anymore. But most of the stuff he had a good name for. That book of eleven songs, he had one called “One for Brucie.” That was my nickname. B-R-U-C-I-E. My mother got this name from a kid on TV that she saw. So the name just kind of stuck with me in my family, but nobody else knows me by that but family members. “Teenie’s Blues” and “Miss Fine,” they were both written for his sister, Leontine LaCoste. She was a pianist and she did the piano bar thing in St. Louis, and they loved each other immensely but would fight like cats and dogs. But both of those — because my aunt was a very elegant person. So that’s why he called her “Miss Fine.” He wrote that big band arrangement of “Miss Fine” for her, and then “Teenie’s Blues” came off the “Blues and the Abstract Truth” album too.
